why: Airflow is the most common orchestrator in data engineering job offers. It schedules pipelines, retries failures and shows what ran when.
outcome: write a DAG with dependent tasks, schedule it, pass data between tasks correctly and debug a failed run.

lessons.title: DAGs, tasks and schedules
text: A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is a pipeline: tasks and the order they run in. Airflow reads Python files in the dags folder and runs each DAG on its schedule.
Each run has a logical date (the data interval it processes). Pipelines should process that interval, not 'now', so re-running an old day gives the same result.
points: schedule='@daily' or a cron string like '0 6 * * *' (every day at 06:00).
catchup=False avoids running every missed interval since start_date.
retries and retry_delay handle temporary failures.
Tasks should be idempotent: running them twice gives the same result.

example.note: TaskFlow API (Airflow 2+). ds is the run's logical date as YYYY-MM-DD.

lessons.title: Operators, connections and passing data
text: Operators are ready-made task types: BashOperator, PythonOperator, SQL operators, cloud transfers. Connections store credentials (database, cloud) outside the code.
Tasks pass small values through XCom (what @task functions return). Large data never goes through XCom: write it to storage and pass the path.
points: Set dependencies with >>: extract >> transform >> load.
Create connections in the UI (Admin → Connections) or with environment variables.
Variables hold small configuration; never put secrets in DAG code.
Use templating ({{ ds }}) to inject the run date into SQL or commands.

example.code:
from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator
from airflow.providers.common.sql.operators.sql import SQLExecuteQueryOperator

download = BashOperator(
    task_id="download",
    bash_command="python /opt/jobs/download.py --date {{ ds }}",
)
aggregate = SQLExecuteQueryOperator(
    task_id="aggregate",
    conn_id="warehouse",
    sql="INSERT INTO daily_offers SELECT '{{ ds }}', COUNT(*) FROM raw_offers WHERE day = '{{ ds }}'",
)
download >> aggregate

lessons.title: Run, monitor and debug
text: The UI shows each DAG run and the state of every task. When something fails, open the task logs first: most errors are a missing connection, a wrong path or bad input data.
After fixing, clear the failed task (and downstream tasks) to re-run only what is needed.
points: airflow dags test <dag_id> 2026-10-01 runs a DAG once locally without the scheduler.
airflow tasks test <dag_id> <task_id> <date> runs a single task.
Backfill re-runs past intervals after a bug fix.
Alert on failure (email, Slack callback) so you are not the last to know.

example.code:
airflow dags list
airflow dags test job_offers 2026-10-01
airflow tasks test job_offers load 2026-10-01

items: c waits for a and b

pitfalls: Heavy code at the top level of the DAG file (API calls, queries): it runs every time the scheduler parses the file.
Using datetime.now() inside tasks instead of the logical date, which breaks re-runs.
Dynamic start_date (datetime.now()) that makes the DAG never run.

exercises.q: Write the dependency line for: extract runs first, then clean and enrich in parallel, then load.
A daily DAG failed for 3 days because of a bug, now fixed. How do you re-process those days?
exercises.answer: Clear the failed runs in the UI (with downstream tasks) or run a backfill for that date range: airflow dags backfill -s 2026-10-01 -e 2026-10-03 <dag_id>. This works because tasks use the logical date and are idempotent.

exercises.q: Write a cron schedule for every Monday at 07:30.

interview.q: What does idempotent mean for a pipeline task?
interview.a: Running it several times for the same interval gives the same result, for example by overwriting the partition for that date instead of appending. It makes retries and backfills safe.

interview.q: What is XCom and when should you avoid it?
interview.a: A mechanism to pass small values between tasks, stored in Airflow's metadata database. Avoid it for large data such as DataFrames or files: write them to storage and pass the path.
Cron only triggers commands at times. Airflow adds dependencies between tasks, retries, backfills, a UI with history and logs, and connections management.
